pos: n. (the first word of the handwriting on Belshazzar's wall)
etymology: Aramaic mene (H4484), numbered, from mena, to count, number; the passive participle appearing twice at the head of the inscription.
biblical_def: Mene is the first and repeated word of the four-word inscription a disembodied hand wrote on the wall of Belshazzar’s feast, in the very hour the king and his lords were drinking from the sacred vessels looted from the LORD’s own temple: “in the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king’s palace” (Daniel 5:5). The full writing reads “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” (Daniel 5:25), and Daniel, refusing the king’s rewards but interpreting anyway, gives the word its plain sense: “MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it” (Daniel 5:26). The doubling of the word is itself part of the verdict’s weight — repetition in Hebrew and Aramaic idiom intensifies certainty, so that the count is not merely taken but settled beyond appeal. The sentence took effect with terrible speed: “in that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain” (Daniel 5:30), the empire passing to Darius the Mede before morning. Mene stands, then, as Scripture’s own vocabulary for the precise, numbered, non-negotiable character of divine judgment — not vague displeasure but an accounting already closed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Mene; it is the Aramaic word, meaning numbered, that opens the handwriting on the wall interpreted by Daniel as God's own verdict ending Belshazzar's kingdom.
webster_full: MENE, n. An Aramaic word meaning numbered, the first word of the divine inscription that announced the fall of Belshazzar's kingdom.
NUMBER, v.t. To count; to reckon; in Scripture, often used of God's exact accounting of days, deeds, or a kingdom's duration.
JUDGMENT, n. The act of judging; in theology, God's righteous verdict upon sin, whether temporal or final.
PROFANATION, n. The act of treating a sacred thing with irreverence or contempt; Belshazzar's use of the temple vessels at his feast.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; in theology, God's absolute right to raise up and cast down kingdoms according to His own will.
scriptures: Daniel 5:25
And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN.
Daniel 5:26
This is the interpretation of the thing: MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.
Daniel 5:27
TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
Daniel 5:5
In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote.
corruption_summary: A judgment scene this specific and this quickly fulfilled, against a king whose very historicity critics once denied until extra-biblical records confirmed him, resists dismissal as later legendary embellishment.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship long treated Belshazzar as a fictional invention of the book of Daniel, since classical historians named Nabonidus as Babylon's last king with no Belshazzar in the record at all — until cuneiform tablets confirmed Belshazzar as Nabonidus's son and co-regent, ruling in Babylon while his father was away, exactly the kind of secondary royal figure a late legend-writer, working from garbled memory generations after the fact, would be unlikely to get right. The book's precision here argues for genuine access to the period, not literary invention.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every kingdom, however great its feast or fine its vessels, stands already numbered before God; Mene is not a threat of future accounting but the announcement that the accounting is complete and the verdict is being executed — the same certainty of judgment Scripture attaches to every soul and every nation apart from Christ (Hebrews 9:27).
roots_summary: Aramaic mene (H4484), numbered, from mena (H4483), to count; teqal (H8625), weighed; peras (H6537), divided; malkuth (H4437), kingdom.
roots_lines: Aramaic mene (H4484) — numbered, the passive participle from mena, to count.
Aramaic teqal (H8625) — weighed; the second word of the inscription, Daniel 5:27.
Aramaic peras (H6537) — divided; the root behind Upharsin, the fourth word.
Aramaic malkuth (H4437) — kingdom; the very thing Mene declares numbered and finished.
Hebrew qets (H7093) — end; the concept Mene enacts for Belshazzar's reign that same night.
usage: “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN” — the full inscription on the wall.
“God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it” — Daniel's interpretation.
“In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain” (Daniel 5:30) — the sentence's swift execution.

pos: n. (a son of Benjamin, also called Huppim among Dan's descendants in Chronicles)
etymology: Hebrew Chuppim (H2650), plural, from chuppah, a canopy, chamber, especially a bridal chamber.
biblical_def: Huppim is named among the sons of Benjamin in the roster of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob: “the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” (Genesis 46:21), his name appearing there in the slightly variant form Muppim. The Chronicler places him, alongside his brother, in a genealogical note whose exact tribal placement has puzzled readers for centuries — “Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir, and Hushim, the sons of Aher” (1 Chronicles 7:12), within a chapter otherwise devoted to Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher, before turning fully to Benjamin’s own line two verses later. A further note ties him to the household of Machir, Manasseh’s grandson: “Machir took to wife the sister of Huppim and Shuppim, whose sister’s name was Maachah” (1 Chronicles 7:15), a rare instance of intermarriage recorded across tribal lines in the patriarchal genealogies. The wilderness census confirms his descendants as a distinct family: “of Shupham, the family of the Shuphamites: of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites” (Numbers 26:39), the same name shifting slightly again in spelling, as many Hebrew names do across the centuries of transmission.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Huppim; he is a son of Benjamin (named Muppim in Genesis) whose family, the Huphamites, is confirmed in the wilderness census and noted again in Chronicles' genealogy.
webster_full: HUPPIM, n. A son of Benjamin, also called Muppim and Hupham, ancestor of the family of the Huphamites.
BENJAMIN, n. The youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, ancestor of the tribe from which King Saul and the apostle Paul descended.
CENSUS, n. An official enumeration of the inhabitants of a country, tribe, or family.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of persons or families from an ancestor.
INTERMARRIAGE, n. Marriage between members of different families, tribes, or nations.
scriptures: Genesis 46:21
And the sons of Benjamin were Belah, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard.
1 Chronicles 7:12
Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir, and Hushim, the sons of Aher.
1 Chronicles 7:15
And Machir took to wife the sister of Huppim and Shuppim, whose sister's name was Maachah;) and the name of the second was Zelophehad: and Zelophehad had daughters.
Numbers 26:39
Of Shupham, the family of the Shuphamites: of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites.
corruption_summary: The honest, unsmoothed spelling variation of one man's name across three books, rather than a suspiciously uniform later standardization, is the signature of authentic transmission across centuries, not invention.
corruption_paragraphs: A skeptical view that treats these genealogical variants (Muppim, Huppim, Hupham) as evidence of textual corruption or careless late compilation gets the logic backward: a forger constructing a genealogy from imagination tends toward artificial consistency, while genuine records transmitted across thirteen centuries by different hands in different books naturally show exactly this kind of minor orthographic drift on minor names, while the tribal and family structure itself remains stable and coherent throughout.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD's own meticulous care for the humblest names in His people's record — a minor son of Benjamin, mentioned only in genealogical lists, is nonetheless counted, spelled with real if imperfect consistency, and preserved across a millennium of Israel's history, a small witness that no name written in the covenant people's record is beneath the LORD's notice (Malachi 3:16).
roots_summary: Hebrew Chuppim (H2650), from chuppah (H2646), canopy, bridal chamber; mishpachah (H4940), family; paqad (H6485), to number, muster.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chuppim (H2650) — from chuppah, a canopy or bridal chamber.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the unit the census organizes Huppim's descendants into.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to number, muster, appoint; the verb behind the wilderness census.
Hebrew ben (H1121) — son; the word introducing Huppim in Genesis 46:21.
Hebrew achoth (H269) — sister; the kinswoman whose marriage to Machir ties two tribal lines together.
usage: “Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard” — his place among the sons of Benjamin.
“Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir” — the Chronicler's genealogical note.
“Of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites” — the wilderness census confirming his line.

pos: n. (a surname or Roman name borne by at least three men in the New Testament)
etymology: Latin Iustus, just, righteous, upright; a common Roman cognomen adopted by several Jewish and Jewish-Christian men of the apostolic era.
biblical_def: Justus is the Latin surname of at least three distinct men in the New Testament, each appearing at a hinge moment in the early church. The first is a candidate to replace Judas among the twelve: “they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias” (Acts 1:23), though the lot fell to Matthias instead (Acts 1:26) — Justus thus stands as a man esteemed worthy of apostleship by the gathered church yet passed over by the LORD’s own sovereign choosing, a sobering pattern for any ambition after office. The second is a Corinthian God-fearer whose house became, after the synagogue’s rejection of Paul’s preaching, the base for the church’s continued work in that city: Paul “entered into a certain man’s house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue” (Acts 18:7), a deliberately provocative proximity that put the new congregation in full view of the old. The third is a Jewish believer among Paul’s few faithful fellow-laborers during a Roman imprisonment: “Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Colossians 4:11) — a man whose given name, Jesus (the same as the Lord’s own, a common Jewish name of the era), Paul quietly passes over in favor of his surname, perhaps out of reverence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Justus as a common Roman name meaning just or upright; the New Testament names at least three different men who bore it, including a candidate apostle, a Corinthian host, and one of Paul's few faithful companions in prison.
webster_full: JUSTUS, n. A Latin surname, meaning just or upright, borne by at least three men in the New Testament church.
APOSTLE, n. One sent with a message or commission; specifically, one of the twelve chosen by Christ, or Matthias and Paul added afterward.
LOT, n. That which happens to a person by chance, or which falls to him as his portion; in Scripture, often used to discern God's will.
PROSELYTE, n. A convert; one who worships the true God though not born a Jew, such as many God-fearing Gentiles of Acts.
FELLOWLABORER, n. One who works together with another in a common cause; Paul's term for his faithful companions in ministry.
scriptures: Acts 1:23
And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.
Acts 18:7
And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man's house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue.
Colossians 4:11
And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me.
Acts 1:26
And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
corruption_summary: Three unrelated men sharing one common Roman surname, each fitting naturally and without confusion into a different, historically plausible setting, is the texture of real record-keeping, not a symbol invented for literary effect.
corruption_paragraphs: Literary-critical readings eager to flatten distinct historical persons into symbolic types miss that Luke and Paul, writing independently, each use Justus as an ordinary contemporary Roman surname attached to ordinary, differentiated men — ancient Jewish adoption of Latin names under Roman rule is well attested outside Scripture, and the casual, non-explanatory way each Justus is introduced argues for straightforward historical reportage rather than deliberate literary patterning.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the Acts 1 Justus especially: being esteemed worthy of the highest visible office in the church by the gathered assembly is not the same as being the LORD's chosen instrument for it, and a man can be genuinely just, genuinely qualified, and still passed over by sovereign appointment — a needed corrective to any ministry culture that equates human esteem with divine calling.
roots_summary: Latin Iustus, just, righteous, upright; Greek dikaios (G1342), just, righteous; kleros (G2819), lot, portion; sunergos (G4904), fellow-worker.
roots_lines: Latin Iustus — just, righteous, upright; a common Roman cognomen.
Greek dikaios (G1342) — just, righteous; the underlying moral sense the Latin name translates.
Greek kleros (G2819) — lot, portion, inheritance; the means by which Matthias, not Justus, was chosen.
Greek sunergos (G4904) — fellow-worker; Paul's title for the Justus of Colossians 4:11.
Greek sebomai (G4576) — to worship, revere; describing the Corinthian Justus's devotion to God.
usage: “Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus” — the candidate passed over for Matthias.
“A certain man's house, named Justus... whose house joined hard to the synagogue” — the Corinthian host.
“Jesus, which is called Justus... my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God” — Paul's faithful companion in prison.

pos: n. (the Old Testament KJV name for the land of the Philistines)
etymology: Hebrew Pəlesheth (H6429), Philistia; rendered Palestina in Exodus and Isaiah, and Philistia elsewhere in the KJV, both from the same Hebrew word.
biblical_def: Palestina is the Authorized Version’s rendering, in three specific places, of the same Hebrew word elsewhere translated Philistia — the coastal land of Israel’s persistent enemy, the Philistines. Moses’s song at the Red Sea names it among the nations who would hear of the Exodus and tremble: “the people shall hear, and be afraid: sorrow shall take hold on the inhabitants of Palestina” (Exodus 15:14), a prophetic anticipation centuries before Israel would actually contend with the Philistines in Canaan. Isaiah returns to the name twice in a single oracle of judgment, given in the year King Ahaz died: “Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent’s root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent” (Isaiah 14:29), a warning that a fallen oppressor’s death is no final relief where greater judgment is still appointed, followed immediately by “Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved: for there shall come from the north a smoke” (Isaiah 14:31). Amos, prophesying against the same coastal cities under their more common name, pronounces an identical sentence in different words: “For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom” (Amos 1:6) — the same land, the same ancient enemy, judged consistently across three different prophetic voices.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Palestina as the ancient name of the country of the Philistines, used by the Authorized Version in Exodus and Isaiah for the same land elsewhere called Philistia.
webster_full: PALESTINA, n. The Old Testament name, in the Authorized Version, for the land of the Philistines, called Philistia elsewhere.
PHILISTINES, n. An ancient people inhabiting the coastal plain of Canaan, persistent enemies of Israel throughout the historical books.
PROPHECY, n. A declaration of something to come, made under divine inspiration; here, judgment pronounced on a specific nation.
OPPRESSOR, n. One who exercises harsh authority; one who wrongs or persecutes others with cruelty and injustice.
GAZA, n. One of the five chief cities of Philistia, singled out in Amos's oracle of judgment.
scriptures: Exodus 15:14
The people shall hear, and be afraid: sorrow shall take hold on the inhabitants of Palestina.
Isaiah 14:29
Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent.
Isaiah 14:31
Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved: for there shall come from the north a smoke, and none shall be alone in his appointed times.
Amos 1:6
Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom.
corruption_summary: Three prophets across different centuries pronouncing consistent, specific judgment on the same coastal people under two interchangeable names is exactly the kind of coherent prophetic tradition a fragmented, late-assembled text is least likely to produce.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical approaches that treat prophetic oracles against foreign nations as generic, formulaic literary exercises with no real predictive content struggle with the specificity across these texts — Isaiah's timing note (“in the year that king Ahaz died,” Isaiah 14:28) ties the oracle to a real, datable moment, and the escalating imagery of a broken rod giving way to a worse serpent matches the actual historical sequence of successive Near Eastern threats to Philistia rather than a vague, timeless curse formula.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own warning against premature relief at a fallen oppressor's death: the removal of one threat is not the removal of judgment itself where deeper covenant unfaithfulness remains unaddressed, a warning as applicable to nations trusting their own strength as to any soul mistaking temporal relief for lasting peace with God.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pəlesheth (H6429), Philistia; Pelishti (H6430), Philistine; tsaphon (H6828), north, the direction of coming judgment; shabar (H7665), to break.
roots_lines: Hebrew Pəlesheth (H6429) — Philistia; the same word rendered Palestina in these three verses.
Hebrew Pelishti (H6430) — Philistine; the people-name behind the place-name.
Hebrew tsaphon (H6828) — north, the direction from which Isaiah's coming smoke and judgment arrive.
Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break, shatter; the fate of the rod that had smitten Palestina.
Hebrew pesha' (H6588) — transgression, rebellion; Amos's governing charge against Gaza and her sister cities.
usage: “Sorrow shall take hold on the inhabitants of Palestina” — Moses's prophetic song at the Red Sea.
“Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina” — Isaiah's warning against premature relief.
“Thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved” — the judgment's fulfillment declared.

pos: n. (a stream or border marker of Egypt, used as a byword for Egypt's power)
etymology: Hebrew Shichor (H7883), possibly "black" or "turbid," referring to the dark, silt-laden waters, commonly identified with a branch of the Nile or Egypt's eastern border wadi.
biblical_def: Sihor marks the southwestern edge of the promised land, named at the head of the summary of territory still unconquered in Joshua’s old age: “from Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines” (Joshua 13:3) — Sihor functions here as shorthand for Egypt’s own border, the point at which the promised land’s southern boundary met the great power to the south. The name carries covenant weight beyond mere geography in Jeremiah’s indictment of Judah’s political idolatry: “what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river?” (Jeremiah 2:18) — seeking security in foreign alliance, symbolized as drinking a foreign river’s water, is treated as spiritual adultery against the LORD, the true fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13). Isaiah invokes the same waters as the very source of Tyre’s and, by extension, the wider region’s commercial wealth: “by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations” (Isaiah 23:3). The Chronicler, describing the ark’s return under David, uses a nearly identical form to mark all Israel’s extent, “from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath” (1 Chronicles 13:5), the same border-marker doing double duty as a measure of the kingdom’s full reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no separate entry for Sihor; it is the Hebrew name, meaning black or turbid, for the waters marking Egypt's border, used throughout the Old Testament as shorthand for Egypt itself and for misplaced trust in foreign power.
webster_full: SIHOR, n. A stream or border marking Egypt, from a Hebrew word meaning black or turbid; used as shorthand for Egypt itself.
EGYPT, n. An ancient and powerful nation of northeastern Africa, called Mizraim in Hebrew, repeatedly a source of false security for Israel.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of false gods; by extension, any misplaced trust or ultimate allegiance given to something other than the true God.
ALLIANCE, n. A union or connection of interests between nations or parties, often condemned in the prophets when made in place of trust in God.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring of water; in Scripture, a common figure for God Himself as the source of life, contrasted with cisterns of human devising.
scriptures: Joshua 13:3

From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites:
Jeremiah 2:18
And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river?
Isaiah 23:3
And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations.
1 Chronicles 13:5
So David gathered all Israel together, from Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath, to bring the ark of God from Kirjathjearim.
corruption_summary: A consistent geographical and theological use of one border-name across Joshua, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Chronicles argues for a unified prophetic-historical tradition rather than disconnected late fragments.
corruption_paragraphs: Fragmentary source theories that treat the historical and prophetic books as unrelated literary strata cannot easily explain why Sihor consistently marks the same geopolitical reality — Egypt's border and Egypt's seductive power — across four books spanning Israel's history from the conquest to the exile, each usage building coherently on the same underlying geography and the same theological point about trusting Egypt over the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own indictment: drinking Sihor's or the Euphrates's water, that is, seeking security in Egypt's or Assyria's alliance rather than in the LORD, is named forsaking “the fountain of living waters” for broken cisterns of human contrivance (Jeremiah 2:13) — a warning against every merely political or worldly solution sought in place of simple trust in God, as current now as in Jeremiah's day.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shichor (H7883), black, turbid; Mitsrayim (H4714), Egypt; mayim (H4325), waters; maqor (H4726), fountain, spring.
roots_lines: Hebrew Shichor (H7883) — possibly black or turbid, describing the dark, silt-laden waters.
Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714) — Egypt; the land Sihor marks the border of.
Hebrew mayim (H4325) — waters; the element Jeremiah uses as a figure for misplaced trust.
Hebrew maqor (H4726) — fountain, spring; the true source Jeremiah says Israel forsook.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, boundary; the geographical function Sihor serves in Joshua and Chronicles.
usage: “From Sihor, which is before Egypt” — the southern border marker of the promised land.
“To drink the waters of Sihor” — Jeremiah's figure for trusting Egypt over the LORD.
“From Shihor of Egypt even unto the entering of Hemath” — the full extent of David's kingdom.

pos: n. (the king of Shinar, one of the four eastern kings defeated by Abraham)
etymology: Hebrew Amraphel (H569), of disputed derivation, possibly Akkadian or Elamite in origin; king of Shinar, the region of ancient Babylonia.
biblical_def: Amraphel opens the roll call of the four eastern kings whose invasion of Canaan draws Abraham into his only recorded military campaign: “in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations” (Genesis 14:1). These four had held five Canaanite kings, including the king of Sodom, under tribute to Chedorlaomer for twelve years before a rebellion in the thirteenth year brought the eastern coalition west in force (Genesis 14:4), the same four named again as they mass against the rebels: “Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and... Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five” (Genesis 14:9). Their victory swept up Lot, Abraham’s nephew, among the captives — the provocation that sent Abraham and his three hundred and eighteen trained servants in pursuit, resulting in a rescue so complete that “the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king’s dale” (Genesis 14:17) — the same meeting at which Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine to bless Abraham. Amraphel is thus part of the earliest recorded international military alliance in Scripture, and the earliest recorded instance of one of the patriarchs directly opposing an imperial coalition in battle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Amraphel; he is the king of Shinar named first among the four eastern kings Abraham defeated in Genesis 14 to rescue his nephew Lot.
webster_full: AMRAPHEL, n. A king of Shinar, one of four eastern kings defeated by Abraham in the rescue of Lot.
SHINAR, n. The ancient region of lower Mesopotamia, later the site of Babylon; the land of Amraphel and of the tower of Babel.
TRIBUTE, n. A stated sum or other valuable thing paid by one ruler or nation to another, in acknowledgment of submission.
ALLIANCE, n. A union or connection of interests between nations, kings, or parties, for mutual advantage or defense.
PATRIARCH, n. The father and ruler of a family; one of the progenitors of the Hebrew nation, such as Abraham.
scriptures: Genesis 14:1
And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;
Genesis 14:9
With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five.
Genesis 14:4
Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
Genesis 14:17
And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king's dale.
corruption_summary: A precisely named four-king eastern coalition, with a specific twelve-year tribute period and a datable political backdrop, is exactly the sort of concrete historical detail a late-invented patriarchal legend has no motive to manufacture.
corruption_paragraphs: Older critical scholarship dismissed Genesis 14 as a late, artificial insertion with no genuine historical background, in part because Amraphel's name was once thought impossible to place in the ancient Near East — a judgment increasingly qualified as cuneiform studies have clarified plausible Elamite and Mesopotamian political configurations of the general era, a pattern of the chapter's details becoming more, not less, historically credible as evidence accumulates rather than less.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Abraham's conduct after the victory: though entitled to the spoil his rescue had won, he refused it entirely from the king of Sodom, “lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich” (Genesis 14:23), while receiving Melchizedek's blessing and paying him tithes — a model of refusing entanglement with worldly power even in the moment of victory over it, and of honoring the LORD's true priest above every earthly king.
roots_summary: Hebrew Amraphel (H569), of disputed derivation; Shin'ar (H8152), Shinar; melek (H4428), king; chalats (H2502), to draw out, rescue.
roots_lines: Hebrew Amraphel (H569) — of disputed derivation, possibly Akkadian or Elamite in origin.
Hebrew Shin'ar (H8152) — Shinar, the ancient region of lower Mesopotamia.
Hebrew melek (H4428) — king; the title borne by all four members of the eastern coalition.
Hebrew chalats (H2502) — to draw out, equip for war, rescue; Abraham's action in pursuing the captors.
Hebrew ma'aser (H4643) — tithe; what Abraham gave Melchizedek immediately after this victory.
usage: “In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar” — the opening of Genesis 14's account.
“Four kings with five” — the scale of the ancient coalition warfare.
“After his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that were with him” — Abraham's decisive victory.

pos: n. (the "ascent of scorpions," a landmark on Judah's southern border)
etymology: Hebrew Ma'aleh Aqrabbim (H4610), the ascent or pass of scorpions, from aqrab, scorpion.
biblical_def: Akrabbim, literally the ascent of scorpions, marks a fixed point on the southern boundary of the promised land, named in the LORD’s own description of Israel’s inheritance through Moses: “your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadeshbarnea” (Numbers 34:4). Joshua’s allotment of Judah’s territory repeats the same landmark in the fuller southern boundary description: “it went out to the south side to Maalehacrabbim, and passed along to Zin, and ascended up on the south side unto Kadeshbarnea” (Joshua 15:3), part of the careful, surveyor’s-precision boundary language that opens “this then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families; even to the border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward was the uttermost part of the south coast” (Joshua 15:1). The name also marks a limit of Amorite territory in the period of the judges: “the coast of the Amorites was from the going up to Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward” (Judges 1:36), the closing note of a chapter otherwise devoted to Israel’s incomplete conquest — Akrabbim standing, in this final verse, as a marker of ground the Amorites still held rather than ground Israel had secured.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Akrabbim; the name means the ascent of scorpions, a fixed landmark on Judah's southern border named in Numbers, Joshua, and Judges.
webster_full: AKRABBIM, n. A pass or ascent on the southern border of the promised land, meaning the ascent of scorpions.
BORDER, n. The outer edge, limit, or confine of a territory or country.
INHERITANCE, n. That which is or may be inherited; in Scripture, especially the land promised and allotted to Israel.
ZIN, n. A wilderness region on the southern border of Canaan, near Kadesh-barnea.
SCORPION, n. A venomous arachnid of arid regions; in Scripture, a figure for painful affliction or judgment (1 Kings 12:11).
scriptures: Numbers 34:4

And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadeshbarnea, and shall go on to Hazaraddar, and pass on to Azmon:
Joshua 15:3

And it went out to the south side to Maalehacrabbim, and passed along to Zin, and ascended up on the south side unto Kadeshbarnea, and passed along to Hezron, and went up to Adar, and fetched a compass to Karkaa:
Judges 1:36
And the coast of the Amorites was from the going up to Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward.
Joshua 15:1
This then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families; even to the border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward was the uttermost part of the south coast.
corruption_summary: Precise, repeatable boundary-survey language matching across three separate books is the mark of a real land-grant record, not the vague geography a late, invented national epic would supply.
corruption_paragraphs: Minimalist approaches to Israel's early history, treating the conquest and settlement accounts as late retrojected literary constructions, have to explain why the boundary descriptions read like actual administrative land-survey documents rather than epic narrative — the fixed, technical, repeated sequence of landmarks from Akrabbim to Zin to Kadesh-barnea across Numbers and Joshua is precisely the kind of dry, unglamorous, checkable detail a late national myth has no reason to invent with this much internal consistency.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD's own precision in fulfilling His promise: the land given to Abraham by covenant (Genesis 15:18) is, generations later, measured out to the exact boundary marker, scorpion-pass and all — the God who makes promises keeps them down to the surveyor's stake, a pattern of exactness that should ground confidence in every less tangible promise of His word as well.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ma'aleh (H4608), ascent; aqrab (H6137), scorpion; gebul (H1366), border, boundary; nachalah (H5159), inheritance.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ma'aleh (H4608) — ascent, going up; the first element of the full name.
Hebrew aqrab (H6137) — scorpion; the second element, giving the pass its vivid name.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, boundary; the surveying term governing the whole passage.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance; the land this border marks the edge of.
Hebrew Emori (H567) — Amorite; the people still holding ground near this landmark in Judges 1:36.
usage: “Your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim” — the LORD's boundary description through Moses.
“It went out to the south side to Maalehacrabbim” — Judah's allotted border in Joshua.
“The coast of the Amorites was from the going up to Akrabbim” — ground still unconquered in Judges.

pos: n. (the father of the prophet Jonah)
biblical_def: Amittai is known to Scripture solely as the father of one of its most memorable prophets, named at the opening of both books that record his son’s ministry: “now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying” (Jonah 1:1), and again in the historical notice of Jonah’s earlier, successful prophetic word to Israel — “he restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gathhepher” (2 Kings 14:25). This second reference is historically significant: it confirms Jonah as a real, datable prophet active in the northern kingdom under Jeroboam II, whose message of territorial restoration actually came to pass, establishing his credentials before the more famous and more reluctant commission to Nineveh recorded in his own book. That commission came not once but twice: “the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying” (Jonah 3:1), after Jonah’s flight and the great fish, repeating the original charge — “arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me” (Jonah 1:2). Amittai’s own name, meaning truthful, stands in quiet tension with his son’s recorded flight from the LORD’s truth-bearing errand, a tension the book of Jonah never resolves except in Jonah’s own eventual, reluctant obedience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Amittai; his name means truthful, and Scripture knows him only as the father of the prophet Jonah, named in both 2 Kings and the book of Jonah.
webster_full: AMITTAI, n. The father of the prophet Jonah, named in 2 Kings 14:25 and Jonah 1:1.
JONAH, n. A prophet of Israel under Jeroboam II, sent to pronounce judgment on Nineveh, remembered for fleeing his commission and being swallowed by a great fish.
PROPHET, n. One who speaks by divine inspiration; one who foretells future events or declares the will of God.
NINEVEH, n. The ancient capital of Assyria, the object of Jonah's reluctant preaching and subsequent repentance.
COMMISSION, n. A charge, warrant, or authority given to a person to act on another's behalf; in Scripture, a divine calling to a task.
scriptures: Jonah 1:1
Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,
2 Kings 14:25

He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the LORD God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gathhepher.
Jonah 3:1
And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying,
Jonah 1:2
Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.
corruption_summary: An incidental historical cross-reference in 2 Kings confirming the prophet named in Jonah's own book, complete with hometown and reigning king, is the kind of unforced corroboration a late, fictionalized parable would not bother to plant.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical readings that treat the book of Jonah as pure parable or late didactic fiction with no historical prophet behind it have to explain away 2 Kings 14:25's matter-of-fact historical notice, written in a wholly different genre and context, naming the same prophet, the same father, and even his hometown of Gath-hepher — an independent historical anchor a deliberately fictional composition gains nothing by including and every reason to omit if inventing the figure from nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's word, given twice to the son of a man named Truthful, does not change between the first commission and the second — the repeated charge to Nineveh in Jonah 3:1 is identical in substance to the first in Jonah 1:2, a reminder that flight from a divine calling delays but does not alter what the LORD has determined to do, and that His patience in repeating the call is itself a mercy to the reluctant messenger, not only to the city awaiting the message.
roots_summary: Hebrew Amittay (H573), from emeth (H571), truth, faithfulness; nabi' (H5030), prophet; dabar (H1697), word; shuv (H7725), to turn, return, repent.
roots_lines: Hebrew Amittay (H573) — truthful, from emeth, truth, faithfulness.
Hebrew emeth (H571) — truth, faithfulness; the root of Amittai's own name.
Hebrew nabi' (H5030) — prophet; the office Amittai's son Jonah held.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word; what came to Jonah, twice, from the LORD.
Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to turn, return, repent; the verb governing both Jonah's own flight and Nineveh's eventual repentance.
usage: “The word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai” — the opening of his son's book.
“Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gathhepher” — the historical confirmation in 2 Kings.
“The word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time” — the renewed commission after his flight.

pos: n. (the Meholathite to whom Saul gave Merab, the wife promised to David)
etymology: Hebrew Adri'el (H5741), "my flock is God," or "God is my help," from eder, flock, and El, God.
biblical_def: Adriel is the Meholathite man who received Merab, Saul’s elder daughter, as his wife after Saul reneged on his own promise to give her to David: “it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul’s daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” (1 Samuel 18:19). Saul’s original offer had been made as an open inducement to reckless valor — “behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD’S battles” (1 Samuel 18:17) — with the text exposing Saul’s real motive in the same breath: he hoped the Philistines, not his own hand, would finish David off, so he never intended to honor the promise. Adriel and Merab’s marriage produced five sons, whose end came in the grim episode of national atonement for Saul’s slaughter of the Gibeonites: “the king took... the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite” (2 Samuel 21:8) — a textual note (Michal here standing for her sister Merab, whom she evidently raised the boys for) that ties Adriel’s family directly into the closing reckoning of Saul’s house, delivered to the Gibeonites and hanged “in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest” (2 Samuel 21:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Adriel; he is the Meholathite who married Merab, Saul's daughter, after Saul broke his promise of her to David, and whose five sons were later delivered to the Gibeonites.
webster_full: ADRIEL, n. A Meholathite who married Merab, Saul's daughter, originally promised to David.
MEROB, n. See MERAB, the elder daughter of King Saul, promised to David but given to Adriel.
GIBEONITES, n. A Canaanite people spared by Israel's oath in Joshua's day, later avenged for Saul's violation of that oath.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or a solemn engagement between men; the breaking of Saul's vow to David sets this account in motion.
ATONEMENT, n. Satisfaction or reparation made for wrong or injury; here, the national reckoning for Saul's sin against the Gibeonites.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 18:19
But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife.
2 Samuel 21:8

But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:
1 Samuel 18:17

And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him.
2 Samuel 21:9

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the LORD: and they fell all seven together, and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.
corruption_summary: The uncomfortable, unresolved textual tension over which sister actually raised the five sons is exactly the kind of loose thread real, unedited historical record leaves and a tidy later invention would smooth away.
corruption_paragraphs: A skeptical eye eager to find contradiction in the Michal/Merab difficulty of 2 Samuel 21:8 misreads the evidence: most conservative harmonizations recognize the verse as referring either to Michal's fostering of her sister's sons or a scribal assimilation of the two sisters' names, a genuine textual-transmission question the ancient scribes themselves did not attempt to paper over. A tradition inventing history from scratch has every reason to keep its women's names straight; a tradition transmitting real, messy family history sometimes does not, and honestly preserves the difficulty rather than silently fixing it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bitter fruit of Saul's broken vow: a king who used his own daughter as a tool to arrange David's death instead produced, a generation later, five grandsons paying for his own later sin against the Gibeonites — the LORD's justice reaching back across a king's whole house, a sober warning that the consequences of covenant-breaking are not always confined to the generation that commits it (Exodus 20:5).
roots_summary: Hebrew Adri'el (H5741), my flock is God, from eder (H5739), flock, and El (H410), God; neder (H5088), vow; naqam (H5358), to avenge.
roots_lines: Hebrew Adri'el (H5741) — my flock is God, from eder, flock, and El, God.
Hebrew eder (H5739) — flock; the pastoral image at the root of Adriel's name.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — vow; the category of Saul's broken promise to David.
Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge; the governing action of the Gibeonites' demand in 2 Samuel 21.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — steadfast love, covenant loyalty; the very thing Saul's vow-breaking violated.
usage: “She was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” — Saul's broken promise fulfilled elsewhere.
“The five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel” — the family's tragic end.
“Only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles” — Saul's deceptive original offer.

pos: n. (a wife of David, mother of his fifth son Shephatiah)
etymology: Hebrew Abital (H37), "my father is dew," from ab, father, and tal, dew.
biblical_def: Abital is named among David’s wives during his seven-year reign in Hebron, mother of his fifth son: “the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital” (2 Samuel 3:4), the notice repeated in the Chronicler’s own list generations later — “the fifth, Shephatiah of Abital” (1 Chronicles 3:3). She belongs to a chapter that carefully names each of the six sons born to David in Hebron by six different wives, opening with the notice “unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess” (2 Samuel 3:2) and closing with the sixth, “Ithream, by Eglah David’s wife” (2 Samuel 3:5). Nothing further is recorded of Abital herself, nor of her son Shephatiah beyond his birth notice — he plays no further role in the narrative of David’s reign, unlike his brothers Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah, whose stories dominate the succession chapters that follow. This very silence is itself instructive: not every child born to a king of promise inherits a recorded destiny, and the covenant line proceeds not through Abital’s son but through a wife married later, in Jerusalem, whose own son would one day sit on the throne.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Abital; her name means my father is dew, and she is one of David's wives during his reign in Hebron, mother of his fifth son Shephatiah.
webster_full: ABITAL, n. A wife of David during his reign in Hebron, mother of his fifth son, Shephatiah.
HEBRON, n. An ancient city of Judah, David's first capital, where six sons were born to him by six different wives.
POLYGAMY, n. The state or practice of having more than one wife at the same time; tolerated but not commended in the Old Testament narrative.
SUCCESSION, n. The order in which one person follows another, especially to an office, estate, or throne.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over His creatures, including which of many sons would inherit a throne.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 3:4
And the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;
1 Chronicles 3:3
The fifth, Shephatiah of Abital: the sixth, Ithream by Eglah his wife.
2 Samuel 3:2
And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
2 Samuel 3:5
And the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.
corruption_summary: A carefully ordered, numbered list of six sons by six named wives, agreeing exactly across two independently compiled books centuries apart, is not the kind of record a loosely assembled legendary tradition typically preserves with this precision.
corruption_paragraphs: Source-critical readings that treat the royal genealogies of Samuel and Chronicles as late, independently invented traditions have to explain their exact agreement here, down to the ordinal numbering of each son and the correct pairing of mother to child across two books compiled under very different circumstances and centuries apart — consistency this precise argues for shared access to a real royal archive, not parallel invention.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sobering pattern Abital's silence teaches: David's kingdom-line advanced not through the firstborn Amnon, nor through the fifth son Shephatiah, nor by human seniority at all, but through Solomon, born later in Jerusalem — the LORD's electing purpose, not birth order or a mother's prominence, determines the line through which the promise runs (2 Samuel 7:12–13).
roots_summary: Hebrew Abital (H37), my father is dew, from ab (H1), father, and tal (H2919), dew; yalad (H3205), to bear, beget; bekorah (H1062), birthright, primacy.
roots_lines: Hebrew Abital (H37) — my father is dew, from ab, father, and tal, dew.
Hebrew tal (H2919) — dew; a frequent Old Testament figure for divine refreshing and blessing.
Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, beget; the verb governing every son's birth notice in this chapter.
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — birthright, primacy; the very thing none of these Hebron-born sons finally inherited.
Hebrew kisse' (H3678) — throne, seat; what would ultimately pass to Solomon instead.
usage: “The fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital” — her single appearance in Samuel.
“The fifth, Shephatiah of Abital” — the Chronicler's matching record.
“Unto David were sons born in Hebron” — the chapter that frames her brief mention.
